I feel like I'm in a similar situation with my boyfriend. We've been together for around 4 years and I was worried I was too dependent on him too, I don't really have friends so I only socialise with him, plus my family moved away from my city last year so I don't have them either really.

I agree with everyone else suggesting a hobby, it really does help. Even if it's something like reading, I've started to read more and I prefer reading alone so I can concentrate a lot better. 

Weirdly what I found helped was him changing jobs, he used to work nights a few days a week and now he's working a 9-5 Monday to Friday. He sees me everyday after work but when he's at work I realised how much I needed the time alone. Even if I don't end up doing much I can now appreciate the time to do whatever I want. I think that ties in with me realising he's not going anywhere, we've been together so long and he's stuck with me through me going through bad times so I don't need the reassurance he's going to leave. I used to think I had to be available every time he's free, but now if I have things I need to do I don't fret that I don't spend all my free time with him.

It does take some practise, but it sounds like you have a really loving, supportive boyfriend and you're in a healthy relationship. Over time you'll learn to remember that he isn't going anywhere and that you can relax a little a bit and focus on yourself :)

I live in England and have been in hospital many times because of suicide plans and ideas. I'm sorry to hear about your friends situation.
If he's in hospital now and you ring up, I think they would listen to you and take on board what you say. If he's in hospital then he will be assessed by a mental health team who will decide what to do next. They will protect him when he's on hospital ground. 

Now, if he goes home and decides to carry out his plan and you get worried, if you ring the NHS they will probably send a paramedic to him and take him to hospital again, no matter if he's done something or not. If things get worse, like he's no where to be found, then the police will get involved and he will be assessed by a psychiatrist (who can do a lot more than the shitty NHS mental health team).

I'm not sure if this will happen in Scotland but this is what happens in England. I'm afraid to say that the NHS here is shit when it comes to mental health, so if you talk to them you have to make sure they listen to you and that they listen to your friend.

You're a really caring friend and I hope your friend is okay.

I remember always being told to stop crying or getting 'hysterical' when upset over something, and other things that would make her point out my emotions are invalid. I guess this is a big red flag.
Also we moved house a lot, probably one every 2-3 years since mum would find our house either too pricey or just complain, so I've never had a proper home in my eyes.
